Question: What does this page say about using success fee agreements and legal aid in Scotland? Quote the key points and follow-up links worth reading.
The page says legal aid is an alternative to funding by a success fee agreement, and you cannot use both at the same time for the same work. If a client has ever received legal aid in the case, SLAB has priority over recovered expenses and, if needed, sums from damages before any success fee is paid. It also says to check early whether any prior stage or related proceedings were legally aided, especially if there is a change of solicitor or funding basis.
✓ quote found in the page: "Legal aid (whether advice and assistance or civil legal aid) is an alternative to funding by way of a success fee arrangement."

✓ quote found in the page: "SLAB has a prior call on any expenses recovered, and (where that is insufficient to extinguish any net liability on the Fund)"
✓ quote found in the page: "SLAB has a prior call on any sums recovered in the claim."

Question: What are the complaint stages, time limits for making a complaint, acknowledgement and response times, and any extensions or consent rules? Quote the key wording exactly.

step.detail:
Question: What does this page say civil legal aid covers, how eligibility is assessed, and how to check or apply? Quote the key lines and any links worth following.
Civil legal aid can help with solicitor costs to prepare a case and speak for you in court, and examples include divorce/ending a civil partnership and disputes about children, compensation for injuries or medical negligence, housing issues, debt or benefits, immigration/nationality/asylum, adults with incapacity, and Fatal Accident Inquiries. Eligibility is assessed by the Scottish Legal Aid Board (SLAB), which checks your financial situation, probable cause, whether public money is reasonable to spend, and whether help is available elsewhere; you usually need a solicitor who does legal aid work to apply, and they send the forms to SLAB. To check or apply, the page says to use the civil legal aid estimator and speak to a solicitor or SLAB; if you're looking for legal advice only, apply for advice and assistance.

Question: What success fee caps does this regulation set? Quote the percentages and the damages bands exactly.
For personal injury or death claims, the cap is 20% for the first £100,000, 10% for the amount over £100,000 but not exceeding £500,000, and 2.5% for the amount over £500,000. The regulation also sets a 35% cap for employment tribunal matters and a 50% cap for any other matter.

Question: What does this leaflet say about when to complain, the two stages, acknowledgement and response times, and SPSO escalation? Quote the key wording exactly.
The leaflet says to complain within six months of the event, or of finding out you have a reason to complain, but no longer than 12 months after the event itself. It sets out two stages: 'early resolution' and 'investigation'; at investigation stage staff must acknowledge within three working days and give a full response within 20 working days. If you are unhappy with the response or how the complaint was handled, the leaflet says to contact the Scottish Public Services Ombudsman (SPSO), but only after the complaint has fully investigated.

Question: What time limit does section 17 set for personal injury actions in Scotland, and how is the three-year period measured? Quote the key wording exactly.
Section 17 sets a time limit of three years for personal injury actions. The period runs, in the ordinary case, "from the date when the injuries were sustained"; for a continuing act, it runs from that date or the date the act ceased, "whichever is the later," and for death cases it runs "from the date of that death."

step.detail:
Question: What does this page say advice and assistance covers, who can get it, and how to apply? Quote the key wording exactly.
Advice and assistance can help with the costs of legal advice from a solicitor if you can't afford it; it can include advice on your legal rights and options, help with negotiations and paperwork, help if you're accused of a crime, and help if you've been asked to attend a children's panel hearing. You can usually get it if the case is covered by Scottish law and you can't afford your legal costs, and you may also qualify if you have low disposable capital, receive certain benefits, or have disposable income below a set amount. To apply, you need to find a solicitor that does legal aid work, and they will talk you through your options and help with the application process.

Question: What does this page say about complaining to the organisation first, the time limit to come to SPSO, and any exceptions? Quote the key wording exactly.
The page says you should complain directly to the organisation first: “Make your complaint directly to the organisation.” It says that after the organisation’s final decision, “you can then bring your complaint to us,” and that stage two should be decided “after no more than 20 working days, unless there is clearly a good reason for needing more time.” The page also says there are exceptions to the two-stage procedure: “there are some exceptions to the two-stage complaints procedure.”

Question: Quote the exact wording on the early-resolution stage target, the six-month/twelve-month complaint deadline, and when to go to the SPSO.
The leaflet says the early resolution stage is called “early resolution” and that if a complaint is straightforward and can be easily resolved, staff will try to sort it out in working days or less, unless there are exceptional circumstances. step.detail:
Question: What does NHS Lothian say happens when you complain, including early resolution, investigation, acknowledgement and response times, and SPSO escalation? Quote the key wording exactly.
NHS Lothian says it aims to resolve complaints “as quickly as possible and as close to the point where the issue occurred.” If a complaint is straightforward, staff will aim to resolve it within five working days; if it is more serious or complex, Stage 2 – Investigation applies and they will “acknowledge your complaint in writing within three working days.” If you remain unhappy after the investigation, “you have the right to refer your complaint to the Ombudsman,” and the SPSO can investigate if the complaint remains unresolved.

Question: What does this page say about the legal time limit and any discretion to take late complaints? Quote the key wording exactly.
The page says the normal limit is one year from when the person first knew of the problem, and that the SPSO would not normally investigate complaints that arrive outside that period. It also says the SPSO may, in certain cases, use discretion where there are “special circumstances” and accept a late complaint.

Question: What does this page say the National Personal Injury Court deals with, any value thresholds or categories, and anything about representation or where claims are raised? Quote the key wording exactly.
The page says the court deals with personal injury actions and motions, and that its procedures are available throughout Scotland, including for people acting on their own behalf. It does not mention any value threshold or special claim categories on this page. It also says that when every party is represented by a solicitor, the electronic motions procedure applies, and that completed settlement forms should be lodged with the Personal Injury Clerk, preferably by email, with specific inboxes for opposed motions, unopposed/consented motions, and other process.

says.detail:
Success Fee Agreements and legal aid - Scottish Legal Aid Board (https://www.slab.org.uk/news/success-fee-agreements-and-legal-aid/)
The page says legal aid is an alternative to funding by a success fee agreement, and you cannot use both at the same time for the same work. If a client has ever received legal aid in the case, SLAB has priority over recovered expenses and, if needed, sums from damages before any success fee is paid. It also says to check early whether any prior stage or related proceedings were legally aided, especially if there is a change of solicitor or funding basis.
Quotes: "Legal aid (whether advice and assistance or civil legal aid) is an alternative to funding by way of a success fee arrangement." | "You cannot contemporaneously enter an SFA as the basis of funding of work and provide legal aid whether in the form of advice and assistance or civil legal aid." | "SLAB has a prior call on any expenses recovered, and (where that is insufficient to extinguish any net liability on the Fund)" | "SLAB has a prior call on any sums recovered in the claim."
Links: here -> https://www.slab.org.uk/guidance-categories/civil-guidance/clawback-and-expenses/expenses/; Civil -> https://www.slab.org.uk/news-categories/all-solicitor-updates/civil/; All solicitor updates -> https://www.slab.org.uk/news-categories/all-solicitor-updates/; MyGov.Scot Legal Aid -> https://www.mygov.scot/legal-aid/

Online Feedback Form – Your Rights & Privacy (https://www.nhslothian.scot/yourrights/online-feedback-form/#)

says.detail:
Civil cases - mygov.scot (https://www.mygov.scot/legal-aid/civil-cases)
Civil legal aid can help with solicitor costs to prepare a case and speak for you in court, and examples include divorce/ending a civil partnership and disputes about children, compensation for injuries or medical negligence, housing issues, debt or benefits, immigration/nationality/asylum, adults with incapacity, and Fatal Accident Inquiries. Eligibility is assessed by the Scottish Legal Aid Board (SLAB), which checks your financial situation, probable cause, whether public money is reasonable to spend, and whether help is available elsewhere; you usually need a solicitor who does legal aid work to apply, and they send the forms to SLAB. To check or apply, the page says to use the civil legal aid estimator and speak to a solicitor or SLAB; if you're looking for legal advice only, apply for advice and assistance.
Quotes: "Civil legal aid could help with the costs of using a solicitor to prepare a case and speak for you in court." | "Examples of civil cases include:" | "Your solicitor can tell you if it's likely you'll get civil legal aid. However, it's the Scottish Legal Aid Board (SLAB) who will assess your application and tell you what you'll pay towards your legal costs." | "Use the civil legal aid estimator to see if you could get civil legal aid and what you might need to pay."
Links: civil legal aid estimator -> https://www.slab.org.uk/new-to-legal-aid/eligibility-estimators/estimator-civil-legal-a…

Prescription and Limitation (Scotland) Act 1973 (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1973/52/section/17/enacted)
Section 17 sets a time limit of three years for personal injury actions. The period runs, in the ordinary case, "from the date when the injuries were sustained"; for a continuing act, it runs from that date or the date the act ceased, "whichever is the later," and for death cases it runs "from the date of that death."

Advice and assistance - mygov.scot (https://www.mygov.scot/legal-aid/advice-and-assistance)
Advice and assistance can help with the costs of legal advice from a solicitor if you can't afford it; it can include advice on your legal rights and options, help with negotiations and paperwork, help if you're accused of a crime, and help if you've been asked to attend a children's panel hearing. You can usually get it if the case is covered by Scottish law and you can't afford your legal costs, and you may also qualify if you have low disposable capital, receive certain benefits, or have disposable income below a set amount. To apply, you need to find a solicitor that does legal aid work, and they will talk you through your options and help with the application process.

says.text: Complain: NHS Lothian. Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh A&E is NHS Lothian public care. Complain first to NHS Lothian’s Patient Experience Team, usually through its online feedback form or by email, phone or post. (one official source)

If that fails: Scottish Public Services Ombudsman. If NHS Lothian’s final complaint answer is not good enough, the independent body is the Scottish Public Services Ombudsman (SPSO). You can only go there after the organisation has given its final decision.

Free help: PASS (Patient Advice and Support Service). PASS gives free, independent help to people using NHS Scotland, including support with raising concerns or complaints about NHS care. (not confirmed yet)

Your records: NHS Lothian. You can ask NHS Lothian for your records through its Request for Records Portal or by sending its Subject Access Request form by email or post. The portal itself needs sign-in or account creation before the request form starts. (one official source)

Clinical guidance: Healthcare Improvement Scotland / SIGN. In Scotland, national clinical guidance for professionals is published through Healthcare Improvement Scotland, including SIGN guidelines. NHSScotland also uses NICE interventional procedures guidance in Scotland. (not confirmed yet)

Paying for help: Scottish Legal Aid Board / mygov.scot. An adult in Scotland may get legal aid for a medical negligence claim, and can also fund a case by a success fee agreement ('no win no fee'), but not both for the same work at the same time. There is also advice-and-assistance funding for early legal advice if you cannot afford it. (not confirmed yet)

trace.detail:
Question: What does this page say about using success fee agreements and legal aid in Scotland? Quote the key points and follow-up links worth reading.
The page says legal aid is an alternative to funding by a success fee agreement, and you cannot use both at the same time for the same work. If a client has ever received legal aid in the case, SLAB has priority over recovered expenses and, if needed, sums from damages before any success fee is paid. It also says to check early whether any prior stage or related proceedings were legally aided, especially if there is a change of solicitor or funding basis.
✓ quote found in the page: "Legal aid (whether advice and assistance or civil legal aid) is an alternative to funding by way of a success fee arrangement."
✓ quote found in the page: "You cannot contemporaneously enter an SFA as the basis of funding of work and provide legal aid whether in the form of advice and assistance or civil legal aid."
✓ quote found in the page: "SLAB has a prior call on any expenses recovered, and (where that is insufficient to extinguish any net liability on the Fund)"
✓ quote found in the page: "SLAB has a prior call on any sums recovered in the claim."

Question: What time limit does section 17 set for personal injury actions in Scotland, and how is the three-year period measured? Quote the key wording exactly.
Section 17 sets a time limit of three years for personal injury actions. The period runs, in the ordinary case, "from the date when the injuries were sustained"; for a continuing act, it runs from that date or the date the act ceased, "whichever is the later," and for death cases it runs "from the date of that death."

You can usually get it if the case is covered by Scottish law and you can't afford your legal costs, and you may also qualify if you have low disposable capital, receive certain benefits, or have disposable income below a set amount.
